extraction.research_question: (1) How much information about personality (Big Five, self-report) is conveyed by the linguistic (LIWC 2015) and vocal (pyAudioAnalysis) features of short, semi-structured voice samples? (2) Do semi-structured voice samples reveal more about some personality traits than others? Secondary benchmarks: depression, age and gender (p.2, lines 148-156; p.4).
extraction.theory: Six potential mechanisms linking voice samples to personality (p.1-2): (1) personality drives what people talk about; (2) personality drives how people talk (e.g., loudness, smoking affecting voice); (3) content of speech affects how others treat the speaker, which affects personality; (4) delivery style affects treatment, which affects personality; (5) and (6) a third variable (education, culture, biology) affects personality and either what is said or how it is said. Background: language-personality links across written and spoken text (Pennebaker et al., 2003; Yarkoni, 2010). Prior voice-personality work used either observer ratings or narrow vocal parameters (p.2). The paper states the mechanisms are not tested (p.7).
extraction.data: Sample: UT Austin Introductory Psychology students in a Synchronous Massive Online Course, Fall 2018 (UT1000 Project). Of 1,342 students who completed a 3-week self-tracking assignment, 1,087 used the smartphone app; 213 (email) and 42 (journal) were excluded because they had no audio (p.2). 992 smartphone students gave 25,163 audio responses (mean 21.32 s; mean 40.28 words) (p.2). Preprocessing kept responses with at least 50 words per Google Speech-to-text, leaving 5,838 responses (p.3). One sample per person was kept (each person's first response with at least 50 words; 64% were their first response) = 614 analytic samples, mean 50.74 s and 92.41 words (SD 73.69) (p.3). Unit of analysis: one voice sample per participant. Table 1 Ns: Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Openness, Agreeableness 545 each (means ~37-46, alpha 0.76-0.89); Depression 485 (CES-D-10, mean 11.26); Age 564 (mean 18.57, SD 1.34); Gender 564 (Female 374, Male 190) (p.3). The text does not explain why the Ns differ from the 614 analytic samples beyond noting different survey completion times (Table 1 note). Predictors: 94 LIWC 2015 dimensions (p.3) and 272 pyAudioAnalysis vocal features (136 per 1-s segment statistic, mean and SD over 1-s segments) (p.3). Outcomes: BFI-2 (60 items, 5-point scale) at end of week two; CES-D-10 about two weeks after the assignment (p.2). Recording prompt: describe your situation and current thoughts and feelings, plus about 10 s of environmental sound (p.2).
extraction.method: Two-stage, automated machine learning pipeline in R 4.1.2 (mlr 2.19.0, mlrMBO 1.1.5) with XGBoost (1.5.2.1) as the learner (p.3-4). Stage 1 (global search): 150 Latin Hypercube hyperparameter configurations, each scored by 10-fold CV; a Gaussian Process surrogate and CMA-ES then propose new configurations for sequential model-based optimization, run for at least 50 cycles (extended while improvement continued) (p.4). Feature set fixed at 100%. Stage 2 (feature selection): nested 10-fold CV within each outer fold, Tree SHAP values for each test sample, a pseudo partial R-squared per feature (R-squared of model with the feature's SHAP removed vs. full model), repeated five times and weighted by error; top-30 features kept per outer fold and XGBoost refit with stage-1 hyperparameters held fixed; performance is the mean over the 10 outer folds (p.4). Evaluation: out-of-sample R-squared for regression defined as 1 minus CV test MSE divided by outcome variance (p.4). For classification, log loss is used rather than AUC, and scored as 1 minus model log loss over intercept-only log loss (p.5). Uncertainty: no standard test fits the repeated selection, so final models were re-estimated with 100-fold CV (about 9% more training data per fold), on the assumption that a generalizable model improves with more data (p.5). Post-hoc: reliability (Cronbach alpha, mean feature test-retest correlation) used to disattenuate performance (Spearman 1961) and to test whether scale reliability predicts model performance (p.7-8).
extraction.identification: None causal. The design is cross-validated out-of-sample prediction only; the authors state that without an experimental design the causal direction of each mechanism cannot be established and most variables cannot be manipulated (p.7, lines 907-913). The generalizability standard is that a model fitted on some people predicts unseen people's self-reported traits from voice data (p.9).
extraction.scope: Population: UT Austin Introductory Psychology students who used a smartphone app (mean age 18.6; 374 female, 190 male in the gender analysis), with self-report personality, depression, age and gender. Era: data collected Fall 2018, published 2022. Context: one standardized, open-ended voice prompt with mixed content and environments (not a lab reading task). The paper does not state the speech language or dialect. Results are described as a conservative estimate for brief (about 92 words), constrained, student-only samples (p.8).

limitations: Samples were brief (mean about 92 words), collected in a constrained context (a class-assignment prompt), and drawn from Introductory Psychology students; the authors call the results a conservative estimate (p.8, lines 1031-1041).
The criterion was self-report Big Five scores, which the authors acknowledge have their own biases; they call for non-self-report validation (p.8, lines 1049-1055).
The 50-word threshold is acknowledged as arbitrary; it was set from a Reddit study (25 words) and doubled (p.3, lines 237-243).

Two-stage modeling: hyperparameters tuned on 100% of features were reused after selecting the top 30, which the authors say may be suboptimal. This likely explains why the joint set underperformed vocal-only for Agreeableness (p.9, lines 1108-1135).
No pooling across tasks: predicted gender, age or depression were not used as features for personality prediction (p.9, lines 1136-1149).
No standard statistical test fits the repeated model and feature selection; the uncertainty approach relies on an untested assumption about 100-fold CV (p.5, lines 528-557).

Feature-level interpretation is heavily caveated: many features, non-monotonic effects, and variance explained is not the same as importance (p.6, lines 631-641). The explanations offered for feature-trait links are described as highly speculative (p.8, lines 1020-1022).
Post-hoc reliability correlation (r=0.80, p=.057) is not robust under leave-one-out (r=0.309) (p.7).
No causal identification and no experimental design; mechanisms in the Introduction were not tested (p.7, lines 907-913).
Ns differ across outcomes (Table 1 note: 545 for Big Five, 485 for depression, 564 for age and gender); the text does not fully reconcile these with the 614 analytic samples (p.3).

Raw voice data may contain personally identifiable information; the authors offer analyses or anonymized features on request (p.9, lines 1191-1194). Supplementary files: FeatureRankings.csv, SHAP_Data.RDS, SHAP_Indicators.RDS (p.6).

summary_md:
Marrero, Gosling, Pennebaker and Harari (2022) took one short smartphone voice sample (mean 92 words, about 51 s) from each of 614 UT Austin intro-psychology students. They used XGBoost with Tree-SHAP feature selection to predict self-reported BFI-2 traits from 94 LIWC-2015 dimensions and 272 pyAudioAnalysis vocal features. The fit metric is out-of-sample R-squared from 100-fold CV, and the paper gives no permutation null. Averaged across the Big Five, the joint feature set explained 10.67% of variance, vocal features alone 6.24% and LIWC alone 3.13%. Extraversion, Conscientiousness and Neuroticism reached 10-20% with the joint set, Openness stayed under 10%, and gender was predicted at over 90%. The authors say the joint result is more than the sum of the two parts, but they give no causal identification and the criterion is self-report.

This paper is not new to the system. It was the stated method source for `big5_audio_faithful_prereg.md` and was cited in Addendum 1 of `big5_audio_prereg.md`. In July 2026 Melange ran three one-look audio tests at N=90 legislators. Two findings partly carried over: a full eGeMAPS-88 ridge predicted Pink-E (held-out r +0.284, perm-p .030) and Pink-ES (r +0.298, perm-p .017). The paper's headline did not carry over. Super-additivity missed every time: vocal added +0.001 over linguistic for E against Pink, and -0.004 over text against behavioural visibility. Voice did not measure C (r -0.081). The A-ES halo got worse (|r| 0.819 and 0.946).

What the paper means for the system as built: it is the benchmark the audio lane has already tested and largely failed to reproduce in legislators. It explains why audio is display-only, and it does not support moving audio into the engine. Two leads remain open. Its top features (MFCC, chroma, spectral entropy, deltas) are mostly missing from eGeMAPS-88. It also shows reliability disattenuation, which the system never applies to its validity coefficients.

summary_issues: Summary says the paper explains why audio is display-only. The paper never discusses display-only status; that decision is recorded in the audio prereg files (big5_audio_prereg.md, big5_audio_faithful_prereg.md).

Summary and paul_alignment say super-additivity missed every time. Three registered bars missed (+0.001 for E, -0.046 for C, and the -0.004 pilot which the faithful prereg calls a strawman design). Round 2 records +0.119 for E over linguistic against visibility as a win, though it is an unregistered context result.

Summary and paul_alignment attribute the make-psychology-load-bearing framing to the paper. The IF-the-pilot-proves-fruitful line is in big5_audio_prereg.md Addendum 1 (line 89), which cites Marrero and Simchon together; it is not the paper's framing.

paul_alignment quotes Paul as saying the system concluded audio is display-only and describes his interest in non-text channels. Neither the quote nor the stated interest was found in the audio prereg files or the brain audio note. Unverified; do not cite as Paul's position.
Summary says the disattenuation tool is never applied to the system's validity coefficients. Not verified in the code read; treat as unverified.
Summary says the three one-look audio tests ran in July 2026. The faithful prereg is locked 2026-07-08; the round-2 run date was not confirmed.

Summary and flags say the top LIWC predictors for N were Analytic and Tone. Table 2 extraction puts function words first in the LIWC column for N, and the paper text names no top LIWC feature for N. Corrected in the affective-N bearing.
Bearing 3 system-side figures for held-out RKH correlations (.21 for O to .51 for E) were not found in the code read or brain notes. Unconfirmed.
gaps_exposed: The paper's top-ranked vocal features (MFCCs, chroma, spectral entropy, delta features) are mostly missing from eGeMAPS v02-88. eGeMAPS has only MFCC1-4 and no chroma, and the round-2 prereg names an MFCC route as untried. Any future audio look could only use a richer feature set if it is pre-registered and kept to a single look, and it would stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

Disattenuation: the paper shows reliability-corrected out-of-sample R-squared roughly triples (E 0.16 to 0.57). The system reports validity coefficients against Pink (reliability about .67) and RKH but does not correct them, and attenuation is mentioned only in prose.

There is no self-report or observer personality criterion for legislators, so a Marrero-faithful self-report replication cannot be run. Pink is the stand-in criterion, and it shares method with the linguistic block, which biases the super-additivity bar against vocal features.

Venue and editing confound: the paper used one unedited smartphone sample per person. The system pools edited broadcast and floor audio with venue effects (disfluency about 26 per 1k words live vs 0.22 on NPR), and that variance is not modelled in the trait tests.

Nothing in the paper, or in the system's audio results, links voice-derived traits to legislative behaviour or lobbying responsiveness. Even if voice measured traits, that would not support feeding them into the receptivity layer.

extraction.title: Who chokes under pressure (Big Five, decision-making)
extraction.venue: Personality and Individual Differences, 74 (2015) 22-28. Texas A&M University. DOI 10.1016/j.paid.2014.10.009 (from the text's header).
extraction.document_type: Journal article, two-experiment empirical study (lab experiments with undergraduates)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in three chunks (lines 0-998), covering title, abstract, introduction, Experiment 1 method and results, Experiment 2 method and results, general discussion, limitations, references, and Tables 1-5 with notes. No Paul markup files existed (the computed task listed "(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Nothing was skipped. The paper has no content on lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators or text measurement.
extraction.research_question: Whether the Big Five personality traits predict who thrives or chokes under pressure during dynamic decision-making, i.e., which traits predict performance decrements under social pressure (Exp 1) and under combined social plus time pressure (Exp 2). Neuroticism was the a priori focus; the other four traits were treated as exploratory (Intro, p. 23; Sections 2.2.3 and 4).
extraction.theory: Trait activation theory (Tett & Guterman, 2000) plus distraction theory (Lewis & Linder, 1997; Beilock & Carr, 2005; Beilock et al., 2004): pressure consumes working-memory resources; neurotic individuals experience more anxiety and intrusive thoughts, so they are more likely to choose the immediately rewarding option.
extraction.data: Experiment 1: N = 127 undergraduates at Texas A&M (76 female, 51 male), course credit. Low-pressure n = 63; high-pressure n = 64 (random assignment, Section 2.1.1). Unit: individual participant, each completing 250 trials. Experiment 2: N = 65 undergraduates (37 female, 28 male), course credit (Section 3.1.1). Three participants were excluded for completion time more than 2 SD from the mean (Section 3.2.1), so the analysed N is about 62. The reported regression df F(5,55) implies N = 61; the paper does not reconcile this. Period: not stated (Psychtoolbox for Matlab v2.5 on PCs).
extraction.method: Lab experiments with a dynamic two-option decision task (Gureckis & Love, 2009; Worthy et al., 2011, 2012). The Increasing option pays less immediately but raises both options' future payoffs, so it is optimal. The Decreasing option pays more immediately but lowers future payoffs. Trial-by-trial foregone payoffs are shown. Dependent variable: average proportion of Increasing-option selections over 250 trials. Personality was measured with the 44-item Big Five Inventory. Experiment 1 analysis: Pearson correlations within each condition (Table 2); a two-step hierarchical regression (Step 1: condition dummy and five traits; Step 2: condition x trait interactions), then separate regressions within each condition to locate the interaction (Section 2.2.3; Table 3). Balance check: t-tests on the five traits by condition, Bonferroni-corrected, none significant at p > .01 (Section 2.2.1). Experiment 2: same task plus a 1705 s time limit with live On Pace / Behind Pace feedback; correlations with completion time and performance (Table 4) and a multiple regression of the five traits on performance (Table 5). There was no low-pressure arm in Experiment 2.
extraction.identification: Experiment 1 identifies the pressure effect by random assignment to pressure condition (social pressure: a fictitious partner and an $8 shared bonus contingent on reaching 16,000 points). Personality is measured, not manipulated, so trait effects are associations, not causal effects. Experiment 2 has no concurrent control: it is compared to the Experiment 1 control sample (Section 3.3, p. 26), and combines social and time pressure, so its trait effects are not randomized. The authors frame Experiment 2 as a replication test of the Experiment 1 neuroticism effect.
extraction.scope: Population: undergraduates at one US university (Texas A&M), recruited for course credit. Era: 2014 data collection (exact dates not stated). Institution: university laboratory. Domain: individual (not group) decision-making in one laboratory task. The authors say results may be limited to the decision-making domain and may not extend to other high-pressure situations (Section 4.1).

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 condition x neuroticism interaction: neuroticism had no significant relation to performance in the low-pressure condition but negatively predicted performance under social pressure.
key_findings.numbers: Interaction DR2 = .06, F(11,115) = 1.96, p = .04; condition x N b = .45, p = .02; high-pressure N b = .50, p < .01; low-pressure N not significant.

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 main effects: pressure lowered performance; neuroticism negatively predicted performance in the first-step model. The first-step model only approached significance.
key_findings.numbers: Step 1 R2 = .10, F(6,120) = 2.14, p = .054; condition b = .43, p = .02; neuroticism b = .25, p = .01; conscientiousness b = .16, p = .09 (trend).

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 correlations within condition: no trait correlated significantly with performance in the low-pressure condition; under pressure, conscientiousness and neuroticism were negatively correlated with performance. The conscientiousness link did not survive the regression and was not replicated in Exp 2.
key_findings.numbers: High pressure: C r = .27, p < .05; N r = .34, p < .01. Low pressure: none significant.

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 agreeableness interaction was a non-significant trend. Higher agreeableness was associated with lower performance under pressure, but not significantly.
key_findings.numbers: Condition x A b = .33, p = .08 (trend); high-pressure A b = .18, p = .17 (ns).

key_findings.finding: Exp 2 (social plus time pressure) replicated the neuroticism effect. Neuroticism and agreeableness both negatively predicted performance; the overall model was significant. Conscientiousness did not predict performance under time pressure.
key_findings.numbers: Model R2 = .19, F(5,55) = 2.61, p < .05; N b = .31, p < .05; A b = .36, p < .01; O, C and E not significant (Table 5 reports b = .16, .16, .06 without significance marks).

key_findings.finding: Exp 2 correlations: agreeableness negatively correlated with performance; neuroticism and conscientiousness were negative but non-significant; completion time correlated strongly with performance.
key_findings.numbers: A r = .29, p < .05; N r = .16 (ns); C r = .16 (ns); completion time x performance r = .62, p < .01.

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 post-task importance ratings did not differ significantly by condition; the low-pressure group rated performance importance slightly lower.
key_findings.numbers: Low M = 4.68 (SD 2.42); high M = 5.17 (SD 2.14); not significant.

key_findings.finding: Authors' overall conclusion: neuroticism is consistently linked to choking under pressure in this task; agreeableness is an unexpected exploratory finding; the conscientiousness result is not supported.
key_findings.numbers: No new numbers; summarizes the above.

measures: Big Five Inventory (BFI), 44 items, 5-point Likert (John, Donahue & Kentle, 1991). Cronbach's alpha .79-.88 (M = .83); convergent r = .73 with NEO-FFI and r = .81 with TDA (Section 2.1.2.1).
Decision-making performance: average proportion of Increasing-option selections across 250 trials (dependent variable in both experiments).

Pressure manipulation: social pressure via a fictitious partner and an $8 bonus contingent on reaching 16,000 points (about 80% optimal choices). Experiment 2 adds time pressure (1705 s limit, live On Pace / Behind Pace feedback).
Post-task importance rating on a 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely) scale (Section 2.1.3).
Total completion time (Experiment 2 only; Table 4).
limitations: Social pressure included a monetary incentive absent from the low-pressure arm, so monetary and social pressure are confounded (Section 4.1).
Neuroticism group means differed between Experiment 1 conditions (low-pressure higher); the authors say this could have skewed results (Section 4.1).
No pressure manipulation check, anxiety or mood measure, or working-memory capacity measure; the working-memory mechanism is inferred, not tested (Section 4.1).
Between-subjects design with no within-subject control of group differences (Section 4.1).
Self-reported pressure did not differ significantly between conditions, and the low-pressure mean was higher than in earlier studies (Section 2.2.1, footnote 1).
Experiment 2 has no concurrent control; it is compared to the Experiment 1 control sample (Section 3.3).
The conscientiousness effect appeared in Experiment 1 correlations but not in the regression, and did not replicate in Experiment 2 (Sections 3.3 and 4).
The agreeableness finding is unanticipated and labelled exploratory (Section 4); its Experiment 1 interaction was not significant.
Sample: undergraduates at one university, individual decisions only; generalization limited (Section 4.1).

Reporting inconsistencies: Experiment 2 mean completion time is 1699 s in the text but 1670 s (SD 55.73) in Table 4; the text's 2 SD cutoff of 292 s does not match Table 4's SD. The Experiment 2 regression df F(5,55) implies N = 61, not the about 62 implied by excluding 3 of 65.
Footnote 2: the 1705 s limit required responses about 25% faster (about 500 ms per trial) than the Experiment 1 average of about 680 ms (Section 3.1, footnote 2).

Beilock, Kulp, Holt & Carr (2004), More on the fragility of performance, J. Exp. Psych: General. Pressure-induced WM distraction.
DeCaro, Thomas, Albert & Beilock (2011), Choking under pressure: multiple routes to skill failure, J. Exp. Psych: General. Pressure enhances WM distraction in the same social-pressure paradigm.

Gureckis & Love (2009), Learning in noise: dynamic decision-making in a variable environment, J. Mathematical Psychology. Source of the decision task.
Worthy, Markman & Maddox (2009), Choking and excelling under pressure in experienced classifiers, Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics. Earlier social-pressure work.

summary_md:
Byrne, Silasi-Mansat and Worthy ran two lab experiments with Texas A&M undergraduates. Experiment 1 had N = 127, randomised to low or high social pressure. Experiment 2 had about 61 to 62 analysed, under social plus time pressure, with no control arm. The task was a dynamic two-choice task in which picking the option that pays less now but more later is optimal. Big Five traits came from the self-report BFI. Neuroticism was the pre-specified trait, and it was the only effect that held in both experiments. In Experiment 1 it had no effect at low pressure but predicted worse performance under pressure: condition x N b = .45, p = .02; added R2 for the interaction step = .06. Experiment 2 repeated it (N b = .31, p < .05). Agreeableness was exploratory. Its Experiment 1 interaction was only a trend (p = .08); it was significant only in the uncontrolled Experiment 2 (b = .36, p < .01). The conscientiousness correlation (r = .27 under pressure) did not survive regression and did not replicate. Extraversion was null. The paper itself flags that money and social pressure are confounded, that there was no manipulation check, and that the working-memory mechanism was never measured.

Why it matters here: this is the citation behind the receptivity layer's susceptibility composite (`.40A + .30N - .20C - .10E`). It reads that composite as how much a legislator moves under lobbying pressure. The paper only partly supports that. Its outcome is worse choices on a delayed-reward task, not giving in to persuasion. Its sample is students, not legislators. Its strongest trait (N) gets a smaller weight than its weakest positive trait (A). The project's own well-powered test of Byrne's mechanism came back null: H5, N x loss domain, partial r = +0.036, n = 441. So the N slot is cited to theory with no validation behind it, and should keep the UNVERIFIED label.

extraction.data: Unit: study/article. N = 80 included articles, published 1982 to September 2024, from 59 journals (Sec 3.3; App. B). Identification: 236 unique Web of Science hits plus 48 snowballed = 284 screened; 83 excluded at title/abstract (82 not relevant, 1 not English); 201 read in full; 121 excluded; 80 included (Sec 3.2-3.3, Fig 1, p.3). Coded on 12 dimensions (Sec 3.4). Per-study sample sizes are not reported in the review except Jankovic et al. (2022), n=27 (Sec 4.1). Authors state they do not have permission to share data.
extraction.method: PRISMA-guided systematic review of Web of Science using AND-combined keyword pairs (Persuasion Strategies/Technologies with Personality Traits/Big Five/Five Factor Model) plus reference-list snowballing (Sec 3.2). Title/abstract then full-text screening; English only; journal ranking not used (Sec 3.3). Deductive coding of 6 dimensions (strategy type, author, moderators, mediators, outcomes, results) plus search term, method, research type, domain; inductive coding of study duration and sample (Sec 3.4). Synthesis is narrative: counts of studies and direction of reported effects. No pooled effect sizes, meta-analysis, or formal quality/risk-of-bias appraisal is described.
extraction.identification: Not applicable: review with no causal identification strategy. The review notes that much of the included research is correlational and that some designs (e.g., Gerber et al. 2013) do not allow firm causal inference (Sec 4.2.4, p.5; Sec 5.3, p.8).
extraction.scope: Population: mainly general population (62.5% of studies) and students (31.25%), patients 1.25% (Sec 4, pp.2-3). Domains: health 41.25%, business 25%, sustainability 7.5% (Sec 4). Era: 1982 to September 2024, most studies 2015-2024 (Sec 3.3). Language: English. Methods: quantitative 91.25%, mixed 8.75%; surveys 80%, field experiments 12.5%, real-world data 1.25%; 80% under 1 hour (Sec 4, p.3). Culture is discussed in Sec 5 but is not one of the 12 coding dimensions.

key_findings.finding: Matching trait-tailored strategies are more effective than non-matching (no strategy); contra-matching (random, non-ideal strategy) is often counterproductive, not merely ineffective. No effect sizes reported.

key_findings.numbers: Count-based narrative; Jankovic et al. 2022 found no significant difference (n=27)

key_findings.finding: Susceptibility differs by Big Five trait: agreeableness most susceptible, neuroticism least.

key_findings.numbers: Table 2: agreeableness High; extraversion Above average; conscientiousness Average; openness Below average; neuroticism Low

key_findings.numbers: n/a

key_findings.finding: Conscientiousness generally average; Halko & Kientz (2010) found it most strongly correlated with responsiveness in health mobile apps.
key_findings.numbers: n/a

limitations: Personality mostly measured by self-report, susceptible to social desirability bias (Sec 5.3 p.8).
Many studies used one-off surveys of perceived persuasiveness; behavioral change not confirmed; field experiments recommended (Sec 5.3).
Dominance of Cialdini's six principles narrows conceptual range (Sec 5.3).
Much research is correlational; relationships may be bidirectional or confounded (Sec 5.3).
Not pre-registered (Sec 3.1 p.2). Journal ranking deliberately not a criterion (Sec 3.3).
Narrative synthesis only: no pooled effect sizes or formal quality appraisal in the text, so the strength of the matching claim cannot be weighed from this paper alone.
Internal conflicts: openness results disagree (Alslaity & Tran 2020 found liking most persuasive for high openness, Sec 4.3.4), and the Table 3 openness row does not clearly match the prose.
Data not shareable per authors (Data availability).
measures: Personality: Big Five / five-factor model (OCEAN), mostly self-report (Sec 2.3; Sec 5.3).
Persuasion strategies: Cialdini's six principles (social proof, liking, authority, commitment and consistency, scarcity, reciprocity) (Sec 2.1).
Outcomes coded: susceptibility to persuasion, perceived persuasiveness, attitude change, healthy eating (Sec 4 p.3; Table 1).
Moderators/mediators coded: Big Five, need for cognition, promotion/prevention focus; customer perceived value, extraverted behaviour, goal facilitation appraisals (Sec 4).

summary_md:
Palm and Tims (2025) is a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 80 studies published between 1982 and September 2024. It asks whether Big Five traits moderate the effect of persuasion strategies, nearly always Cialdini's six principles. Most included studies are one-off self-report surveys of perceived persuasiveness. Samples are mainly the general public (62.5%) and students (31.25%), and the main domains are health (41.25%) and business (25%). The synthesis is narrative only: it counts studies and their reported directions, with no pooled effect sizes and no risk-of-bias appraisal.

**Main claims:**
- Strategies matched to a trait outperform no strategy, and mismatched strategies can backfire.
- Ranked by susceptibility to persuasion, agreeableness is highest, then extraversion, conscientiousness and openness, with neuroticism lowest (Table 2).
- Even so, one included study (Oyibo & Vassileva 2019) found neuroticism the trait most consistently correlated with responsiveness to social-influence strategies.
- Only a few political studies are included (Zarouali 2022, Gerber 2013, Decker & Kramer 2023), and they disagree.

**Why it matters here:** the receptivity layer turns personality into a single susceptibility scalar. Neuroticism gets a positive weight (+.30) and extraversion or dominance a negative one (-.10). The review's ranking runs against both signs, while it supports the +.40 agreeableness slot. The caveat is that the constructs differ. Byrne's composite, which the code cites, is about decisions breaking down under pressure, not about responding to a persuasion message. The review's evidence also comes from consumers and students, not legislators. So the review is weak evidence against the N and E signs, not a calibration source.

**What it exposes:** the engine has no strategy dimension. It models one generic pressure, so the review's main result, which is about matching a strategy to a trait, has nothing in the system to attach to. This analysis is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Count-based susceptibility ranking across 80 studies: agreeableness High, extraversion Above average, conscientiousness Average, openness Below average, neuroticism Low (least susceptible). No pooled effect sizes.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.1; Table 2 p.4; Sec 4.2.1-4.2.5 pp.4-5
bearings.system_side: The susceptibility composite has the same structure on both bases. Lexical basis: susc_trait = .40A + .30N - .20C - .10E. Live default (RECEPT_TRAITS=behavioral, RECEPT_N=affective, RECEPT_COOP=v2): .40 coop_v2 + .30 affective_N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance. The code cites Byrne 2015 choking-under-pressure for N, and states that the C and E dampeners are design priors, not Byrne findings.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak transfer. The review measures response to persuasion messages in consumers and students, using self-reported traits and perceived-persuasiveness outcomes in health and tech settings. The system's N slot is choking under pressure (Byrne), a different construct, and members' traits are read from text or behaviour, not self-report. The review supports the positive A or cooperation weight. It cuts against the positive N weight and gives no support to the negative E or dominance weight. It cannot set magnitudes because it reports no effect sizes. Neither sign change is recommended on this evidence alone: changing weights moves ranks and is a gated recalibration, which is Paul's call.

gaps_exposed: The engine has no strategy or appeal-type dimension. Lobbying pressure is a single scalar, so the paper's central result, that strategies should match traits and mismatches can backfire, cannot be represented. A wrong approach can only reduce gain, never cause a negative effect.
Peer or social-proof influence (edge_mult) and direct pressure (susc_mult) share one susceptibility scalar. The review hints that the N sign may differ between those two channels.

The signs of the N, C and E or dominance weights in the susceptibility composite have no literature support for persuasion as opposed to choking under pressure. This review weakly opposes the N and E signs, and nothing in the system tests them against a behavioural outcome. The H2 prospective contract is unspent.

There is no context or domain moderator. The review finds that openness and extraversion effects change sign across contexts (education, voter mobilization, political microtargeting), while the system applies one fixed composite across all CU issues.
flags: Terminology clash: the paper's 'reciprocity' is Cialdini's message strategy (returning favours). It must not be cited as evidence for the system's competitiveness and reciprocity assumption, which remains NOT validated (D-104..D-108).

Do not use the Table 2 susceptibility ranking as a weight calibration source. It is a count-based narrative synthesis with no effect sizes, Table 3 is garbled, and openness results conflict within the paper.

The review's evidence comes from consumers and students, with self-reported traits and perceived-persuasiveness outcomes. The system has no validated N susceptibility signal (Nokken-Poole MISS; H5 null), and the psych audit reports 3/5 traits validated. Any claim built on this paper needs a status label and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
Any change to the receptivity weight signs moves ranks and needs a ruling from Paul. PERSONA_W 0.30 is kept by owner ruling and is not questioned here.
paul_alignment: The paper partly supports Paul's framing ("very agreeable, or submissive to authority ... should be very susceptible", quoted at receptivity_layer.py:11): agreeableness is the most persuadable trait in the review, which supports the +.40 A or cooperation slot. It cuts against the second leg of his susceptibility composite. The review ranks neuroticism least susceptible to persuasion, and gives extraversion above-average susceptibility rather than resistance. The code is already honest that the C and E dampeners are design priors, and the N weight rests on Byrne's choking result, a different construct from persuasion. His position note for the receptivity layer (traits placed as edge parameters, Oropeza; 10 personalities collapse into 4) does not engage this literature, and he has no annotation on this paper. In this respect his note is not stale, since it never made a claim this review could overturn. The live system has moved further from Big Five text traits to behavioural proxies (coop_v2, affective N, diligence, dominance), which weakens any direct transfer.

related.why: Byrne is the cited source for the positive N weight, based on N degrading decisions under pressure. Palm & Tims rank N least susceptible to persuasion. Same trait, opposite practical direction, because the two constructs differ.
Provides the agency and communion measurement that feeds the persona channel. Palm & Tims give weak evidence on whether communion and agency should raise or lower susceptibility.
Quantifies the returns to political microtargeting, which tests the practical claim (profile, then match) that Palm & Tims assert without effect sizes.
Studies personality-tailored political messaging made with generative AI, the frontier Palm & Tims point to through Matz et al. 2024.
A survey of behaviour-aware influence maximization, cited by the receptivity layer for seed_prob. Palm & Tims supply the trait-moderation evidence that such models assume.
Palm & Tims rely on self-reported traits. Koutsoumpis meta-analyses how weakly text-based (LIWC) traits track self-reports, which limits any transfer to the system's text-derived traits.

backlinks.why: Palm reviews personality as a moderator of persuasion, the monadic receptivity question. Selfhout shows that in tie formation the pairwise similarity effect outweighs individual levels.

meta.title: Measuring stance dynamics in political debate using temporal graph neural networks
meta.venue: Information Processing and Management, vol. 63, article 104705 (published online 4 March 2026; open access, CC BY). Metadata hint corrected: full author names, volume and article number, and DOI taken from the text.

extraction.title: Measuring stance dynamics in political debate using temporal graph neural networks
extraction.venue: Information Processing and Management, vol. 63, article 104705 (published online 4 March 2026; open access, CC BY). Metadata hint corrected: full author names, volume and article number, and DOI taken from the text.
extraction.document_type: Journal article (empirical ML / computational social science, Twitter stance inference)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in three chunks covering all 1,134 lines of the extracted text (lines 0-399, 400-849, 850-1133), including abstract, introduction, related work, methods (Sec. 3, Eqs. 1-12, Algorithm 1), experiments (Sec. 4), stance-shift analysis (Sec. 5), discussion, limitations (Sec. 6.1), CRediT and data statements, and the full reference list. Paul's markup: no markup files were supplied (the task listed none), so paul_markup is empty. Not in the text file: supplementary material (Figs. S1-S2, Tables S1-S4), so the 5-fold CV table, the baseline gap in Fig. 2, and the per-period counts are not available here. Figures 2, 4, 5 and 6 are described only in the text, so their plotted values are not extracted. Page locations use the journal page footers. Relevance check: no lobbying, path-finding, allocation or legislator-level content; elections appear only as the referendum context; networks appear as user-hashtag and user-user graphs; text measurement appears as hashtag-based stance labels and FastText embeddings. Those topics are covered only as they bear on stance measurement.
extraction.research_question: Can a temporal graph neural network infer user-level stance (favor vs. against) toward a referendum from user-hashtag and user-user interaction graphs at each 28-day period, including users who never post about the target, and can the resulting trajectories characterize opinion shifts at population, individual and neighborhood levels? (Sec. 1.1, p.2-3.)
extraction.theory: Opinion change is treated as incremental, path-dependent and embedded in social context rather than abrupt reversal (Sec. 6, p.16). The model is motivated by social-influence and network-evolution theory (Flache et al., 2017; Bianchi & Squazzoni, 2015) and by the claim that inactive "silent" users keep stance information through embedding persistence across snapshots (Sec. 2 and 6). Social influence and homophily in temporal movement are asserted in the discussion (p.15-16) but are not tested beyond descriptive correlations. No formal opinion-dynamics model is estimated.
extraction.data: Two Twitter (now X) datasets on the Chilean constitutional referendums, drawn from users following 384 Chilean news outlets, self-reported in Santiago, with at least 10 tweets across topics (Sec. 3.2, p.4-5). Original pool of about 9.2M users. Entry_DS (referendum of 25 Oct 2020): period 1 Jan to 24 Oct 2020; 849,171 tweets; 12,237 users; 171,615 hashtags; 80 labeled referendum hashtags (23 support, 57 oppose) used by 5,540 users; 11 periods of 28 days. Exit_DS (referendum of 4 Sep 2022): period 1 Jan to 3 Sep 2022; 356,214 tweets; 4,934 users; 57,211 hashtags; 106 labeled hashtags (50 support, 56 oppose) used by 1,897 users; 9 periods of 28 days (Table 1, p.5; Sec. 3.4, p.6). Unit of analysis: user-period snapshot (user stance per 28-day window). Totals across both datasets: about 1.21M tweets and 17,171 user rows (not deduplicated). Ground-truth stance comes from labeled-hashtag interaction counts (Eqs. 1-2). More than 95% of users interact with hashtags from one side only (p.6). Human validation: 100 user snapshots per dataset, two annotators (p.6-7). Word embeddings: FastText CBOW trained on all user-generated content, with preprocessing (Sec. 3.2). Data availability: "on request" (p.17).
extraction.method: TWLGCN (Temporal Weighted LightGCN), an extension of WLGCN (Zhou & Elejalde, 2024). Each 28-day snapshot is a bipartite user-hashtag graph with count-weighted edges (Sec. 3.3). Four GCN propagation layers with symmetric degree normalization (Eq. 3), then multi-head attention over layer outputs (Eq. 4). User embeddings go to an MLP classifier with batch norm and dropout. Loss = focal loss (Eq. 5-6, class imbalance) + lambda1 * SSCL + lambda2 * ||H0||^2 (Eq. 11), with lambda1 = 1e-3 and lambda2 = 1e-6 (Sec. 4.1). SSCL, the Supervised Stance Contrastive Loss (Eq. 9-10), treats same-stance users and hashtags as positives and uses the adaptive reweighting alpha(x) = (rho + x)^(-lambda) from DynaDeno (Eq. 8). Noise-based augmentation of embeddings (Eq. 7). Sequential warm start: Xavier initialization at t=0; later periods inherit embeddings and MLP weights; hashtag initial embeddings from period-specific FastText (Sec. 3.3). User-user graphs: Pas (static follower/friend edges) and Act (per-period directed mention/quote/reply edges, Sec. 3.6, Eq. 12). Adam optimizer; max 1000 epochs; early stop after 50 epochs without validation macro-F1 gain. Stance probabilities from hashtag counts: p+ = |R+| / (|R+| + |R-|) (Eq. 1); ties are assigned by larger count, and ambiguous users are kept in training (p.6).
extraction.identification: Not a causal design. Leakage control: 5-fold CV on annotated users (80% train / 20% validation). For every validation user, all edges to referendum-labeled hashtags are removed before training and inference, so validation users are "referendum-silent" (Sec. 4.1, p.9). Macro-F1 is computed per period on that period's active validation users. Shift analysis (flip categories, t-SNE distances, neighbor-dynamics heatmaps) is descriptive. Neighbor correlations are described as "potential social influences" (p.14) but no identification strategy is applied. Validation of labels: Cohen's kappa for human vs. human and human vs. hashtag labels (p.7). Open concern (not addressed in the text): FastText embeddings are trained on all user-generated content (Sec. 3.2), which may include validation users' text, and the paper does not say whether that text was restricted to training users.
extraction.scope: Population: Twitter/X users in Santiago, Chile, who follow Chilean news outlets and meet activity filters (not representative; the authors say Twitter leaned liberal and supportive of the process, p.12). Institution: the two national constitutional referendums (2020 entry, 2022 exit). Era: January 2020 to September 2022, in 28-day periods. Language: Spanish hashtags (cultural use noted as a generalizability concern, p.16). Scope limited to a single platform and two referendums; no other elections, legislators, lobbying or policy venues.

key_findings.finding: TWLGCN variants keep macro-F1 steady across periods, while the non-TWLGCN baselines (WLGCN, EvolveGCN, DynaDeno) fluctuate much more sharply.
key_findings.numbers: Steady 70%-90% macro-F1 over observed periods; exact baseline values are in Fig. 2 and Table S4 (supplement, not in text).

key_findings.finding: The abstract claims the model beats network-based baselines in macro-F1 by more than 5% at each period using only 0.2% labeled hashtags. The main text does not report the baseline gap numerically, so the claim cannot be checked from the text.
key_findings.numbers: Claimed >5%; labeled hashtags 80/171,615 (about 0.05%) in Entry_DS and 106/57,211 (about 0.19%) in Exit_DS (Table 1, p.5).

key_findings.finding: Carrying embeddings forward across snapshots matters: the full model beats the discrete variant that re-initializes embeddings each period.
key_findings.numbers: On Exit_DS, the full TWLGCN outperforms the discrete variant by 1.3% to 9.8%.

key_findings.finding: Adding active user-user relations (mentions, quotes, replies) gives the best overall performance. Passive follower/friend relations add little, and combining both does not help.
key_findings.numbers: Act improves the base model by about 3% on both datasets.

key_findings.finding: The supervised contrastive loss (SSCL) adds accuracy on top of focal loss. The authors attribute this to same-class contrastive signal.
key_findings.numbers: TWLGCN vs. TWLGCN w/o SSCL: about 2% gain in macro-F1.

key_findings.finding: Human annotators agree substantially with each other on the stance of user snapshots, and with hashtag-derived labels, which supports hashtags as a stance proxy.
key_findings.numbers: Human-human Cohen's kappa 0.836 (Entry_DS) and 0.842 (Exit_DS); human vs. hashtag-derived kappa 0.81 to 0.94; 100 user snapshots per dataset.

key_findings.finding: Population-level stance: the Entry_DS median stays slightly positive (about 0.2) with a small IQR. The Exit_DS median starts below zero and drifts toward positive values, with a widening spread near the referendum date.
key_findings.numbers: Entry_DS median about 0.2; opposing views about 25% of users; Exit_DS median initially negative (no exact value given).

key_findings.finding: Sudden flips between opposing and supporting: the number of O-to-S and S-to-O flips mirror each other across periods, with a sharp rise in supporter-to-opponent flips between periods 7 and 8 in Entry_DS.
key_findings.numbers: No exact counts given in text.

key_findings.finding: Flipping users move in the expected direction in embedding space relative to the annotated-hashtag centroids (periods 10 and 11, Entry_DS).
key_findings.numbers: O-to-S users increase average distance from the opposing-hashtag centroid by over 28%. S-to-O users reduce distance to the opposing centroid by over 10% and increase distance to the supporting centroid by 27%.

key_findings.finding: Neighbors' stance shifts are correlated: users tend to shift in the same direction as their 1-hop and 2-hop neighbors (diagonal dominance). Authors describe this as tight-knit communities moving together; it is a descriptive correlation, not a tested influence effect.
key_findings.numbers: Heatmap values only in figure; no numeric summary in text.

key_findings.finding: Coverage of users present from the first snapshot (users remain predictable in later snapshots even with no activity).
Filtering did not distort the temporal or activity distribution of tweets relative to the raw data.
key_findings.numbers: Cosine similarity > 0.99 and Jensen-Shannon distance < 0.05 for both datasets.

key_findings.finding: Ambiguous users (interacting with both sides) are kept in training because they sit on the semantic boundary.
key_findings.numbers: More than 95% of users interact with one side only.

key_findings.finding: Window length: 28-day windows are chosen by a sensitivity analysis. Shorter windows fragment the graph (low giant-component fraction); longer windows mask rapid polarity shifts.
key_findings.numbers: M = 28 days; 11 periods (Entry_DS) and 9 periods (Exit_DS).

measures: Macro-F1 per period on contemporaneous validation users (primary metric; chosen over accuracy because of class imbalance)
Stance probability per user per period (MLP output, described as in [-1, 1]); the mapping from MLP probability to that scale is not defined in the text
Stance shift delta p between consecutive periods, classified into seven dynamics (static via med + MAD threshold; O->MO, O->LO, O->S, S->O, S->LS, S->MS) (Sec. 5.2, p.13)
Hashtag-derived stance probabilities from interaction counts p+ = |R+|/(|R+|+|R-|) (Eq. 1)
Cosine similarity between user and hashtag embeddings; top-100 nearest hashtags per user and per annotated hashtag (Sec. 4.3.2)
Centroid distances in embedding space, visualized with t-SNE (100-dimensional representations)
Cohen's kappa for human-human and human-hashtag agreement
Giant connected component fraction (window-length sensitivity)
Neighbor-dynamics distribution per category, 1-hop and 2-hop (Sec. 5.2.2)
Jensen-Shannon distance and cosine similarity for filtering-bias check
limitations: Supervision is narrow: stance labels come only from a small set of referendum hashtags (80 and 106 labeled), so users who avoid those hashtags can only partly be validated (Sec. 6.1, p.16).
Labels are hashtag-derived proxies, with human agreement checked on only 100 snapshots per dataset (Sec. 3.4, p.6-7).

Generalizability: one platform (Twitter/X), two Chilean referendums, Spanish hashtags with cultural use; replication across platforms, elections and languages is needed. Hashtag hijacking is not systematically evaluated (p.16).
Fixed 28-day windows: shorter windows are sparse, longer ones over-smooth event-driven shifts; adaptive windows or continuous-time TGNNs are left for future work (p.16).
Sequential warm-start training (DTDG, online) rather than joint end-to-end temporal optimization, which the authors call a trade-off in favor of streaming use (p.17).
Sample is not representative: Santiago self-reported users following Chilean news outlets; Twitter leaned liberal and mostly supportive of the process (p.12).
Vote outcomes are compared only qualitatively (the entry vote passed, the exit vote did not); no quantitative validation against the vote or polls (p.12).
Neighbor-correlation and 'influence' claims are descriptive; the authors say leaders of shifts are future work (p.15).
Main-text performance gap versus baselines is not given numerically; full CV results are in the supplement (Table S4), not in the extracted text.
Data available only on request (p.17). Multimodal inputs, multitask learning and LLM-based user-level stance are unexplored (p.17).

summary_md:
Zhou and Elejalde build TWLGCN, a temporal graph network that infers whether a Twitter user favours or opposes a referendum. It works on a user-hashtag graph rebuilt every 28 days, plus optional user-user edges. The model is trained on only 80 to 106 hashtags labelled by side, from Chile's 2020 and 2022 referendums (about 1.21M tweets; 12,237 and 4,934 users). Each period's embeddings carry into the next. This beats re-starting each period by 1.3% to 9.8% on the 2022 dataset. Mention, quote and reply edges add about 3% macro-F1; follower edges add little. Labels taken from hashtags agree with human coders (kappa 0.81 to 0.94, on 100 snapshots per dataset). The second half is descriptive: seven classes of movement per transition, with a "static" band of median + MAD; flip curves that mirror each other; and neighbours who tend to shift in the same direction (Fig. 6). There is no null baseline and no causal test.

This matters because `fec/stance/stance_dynamics.py` is an explicit port of this paper, without the GNN. It uses 91-day windows on the CU press corpus, carries a member's last stance through silent windows, uses the seven-dynamics taxonomy, tests whether neighbours move together, and proposes stances for silent members from their neighbours. Checked against the live output (`data/stance/stance_dynamics.json`), the port has three problems. The paper's static band assumes a continuous probability. On pooled stance signs it comes out at 0.708, so almost every move counts as static. The neighbour co-movement test is null (134 same / 122 opposite, 52%). The 77.5% sign agreement for imputation (n=1,087) has no party or majority-class baseline, while the paper scores with macro-F1 because its classes are imbalanced. The paper backs the design ideas. It does not validate carrying a label forward, the 91-day window, or the imputation. All of those remain UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: Stance is tracked as a trajectory over 28-day snapshots, with embedding persistence so silent users keep a stance. Movement is sorted into seven dynamics using a static band of median plus MAD. Mirror-image O-to-S and S-to-O flip curves suggest external events. Users with no direct stance are predicted through graph propagation over their neighbours.
bearings.system_side: Module docstring (lines 3-21) states the transplant. Code confirms 91-day default windows (line 26), last observed stance carried through silent windows (lines 48-55), the seven-dynamics classifier (lines 64-67), flip curves (lines 72-84), cosponsor and HCoI co-movement (lines 94-120), and CSV-only imputation proposals that leave the matrix untouched (lines 132-151). Re-run on the press CSV in scratch: 2,388 rows, 373 members, 18 windows.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The design vocabulary transfers. The paper says the mirror symmetry suggests external events; it does not establish an event detector the module can rely on. The paper's neighbour inference is GNN message passing over learned embeddings, not a copy rule, so the system's neighbour-based imputation is an analogue only.
bearings.verifier_note: Trajectory framing, persistence, the seven dynamics and mirror curves are all in the paper text. Softened wording: the paper says the mirror symmetry suggests external events, and that unlabelled users get predictions from graph structure rather than explicit neighbour inference. The module matches its description. The static-band and imputation points are handled in bearings 2 and 4.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation|Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation]]

bearings.paper_claim: The median plus MAD static band is applied to continuous stance values p in [-1,1] from the MLP, computed over all users' absolute changes. The paper gives no condition that users must post in nearly every period; its 10-tweet filter only implies about one interaction per snapshot on average.
bearings.system_side: Band is computed on observed-to-observed transitions only, from confidence-weighted means of stance_sign in {-1,0,+1}, floored at 0.05 (code lines 56-63). Live static_band 0.7076 is reproduced. Of 2,989 transitions, 2,737 (91.6 percent) are static and 252 move: S-to-O 111, O-to-S 43, S-to-MS 88 (a move with no sign change), S-to-LS 7, O-to-LO 2, O-to-MO 1 (flip_curves in stance_dynamics.json, matching the scratch re-run).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The band means what the paper intends only where stance is continuous and densely observed. With pooled quarterly signs it mainly measures how coarse the labels are. The paper gives no support for the seven-class counts. The within-side classes are rare because a move must exceed about 0.71 on a [-1,1] scale; they are not empty by construction.
bearings.verifier_note: The band value and the 91.6 percent static share reproduce. The rel claim that only near-sign reversals register as movement is wrong: S-to-MS (88, no sign change) is the second-largest moving class after S-to-O (111). The claim that the paper's band presumes users who post in nearly every period is not in the paper.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation|Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation]]

bearings.paper_claim: Neighbour co-movement: users shift in the same direction as their 1-hop and 2-hop neighbours (diagonal dominance in Fig. 6). The authors describe tight-knit communities moving together, call it a descriptive correlation, and report no null model and no identification. The text gives no numbers; values appear only in the heatmaps.
bearings.system_side: Co-movement counts same versus opposite direction for neighbours who both move in a window. Diagonal dominance is declared above 0.55 (code line 106). Cosponsor result as stored: same 134, opposite 122, 52.3 percent, below threshold, so null. The HCoI figure of 49 percent cited in the rel is not stored in stance_dynamics.json. Scratch re-run on the current press_hcoi.json gives same 302, opposite 296, 50.5 percent, also below threshold. No permutation or common-shock control exists.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's result is a descriptive correlation at 28-day resolution on Twitter, not evidence of influence. Do not carry the paper's potential social influences wording or its asymmetric social influence signals claim into system text. A null on one layer is a null on that layer only.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper text verified, including the no-null-model caveat. The cosponsor figure reproduces from the stored JSON. The 49 percent HCoI figure does not reproduce (50.5 percent on the current community file), so cite the reproduced value or mark the earlier figure UNVERIFIED. Both values are null under the ad hoc 0.55 rule.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation|Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation]]

bearings.paper_claim: Silent-user inference is validated with 5-fold cross-validation over annotated users. For validation users, all edges to referendum-labelled hashtags are removed before training and inference. Scoring is macro-F1 per period on that period's validation users, chosen over accuracy because of class imbalance. Reported TWLGCN levels are steady between 70 and 90 percent.
bearings.system_side: Imputation takes the mean tier score of at least 5 cosponsor neighbours (MINNB=5, line 132) and keeps blank member-issue cells with |est| at least 0.75 (CONF, line 132). Masking check compares the neighbour estimate sign with the known label sign on confident cells only: 77.5 percent on n=1,087 (stance_dynamics.json). Proposals: 307 (CSV has 308 lines including header). True Neutral (score 0) counts as a negative sign (line 143). The final print says at least 3 informative neighbors while the threshold is 5 (line 152). No party-only or majority-class baseline, no macro-F1, no retraining, no 5-fold split.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's protocol retrains a model with masked own-edges and reports macro-F1 across folds. The system's check is a neighbour-only estimate scored by raw sign agreement on a confidence-selected subset. Call it an analogue. The 77.5 percent is not comparable to the paper's macro-F1 range and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a party or majority baseline is run.
bearings.verifier_note: The paper protocol is stated accurately. The code comment calling the check 'their protocol' overstates the match. The bearing omitted that the 77.5 percent is conditioned on |est| at least 0.75, which is added here.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation|Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation]]

bearings.paper_claim: Carrying learned embeddings and MLP weights forward between snapshots beats re-initialising each period, by 1.3 to 9.8 percent on Exit_DS. The 28-day window was chosen by a sensitivity analysis on giant-component fraction: shorter windows fragment the graph and longer ones mask rapid shifts.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 3.3 p.5 (sensitivity in Fig. S2, supplement); Sec. 4.3.1 p.10
bearings.system_side: Persistence carries the last observed raw stance into silent windows (lines 48-55), not learned embeddings. Carried windows also enter transition counts (lines 69-73), which inflates static counts and credits flips to the window where posting resumes. The 91-day default (line 26) is justified by an analogy comment about quarters, with no sensitivity run.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's persistence gain is for warm-started learned representations that keep updating from new edges. It does not support freezing a categorical label. The window rule can be borrowed, but it needs per-window graphs the press corpus does not supply. Fig. S2 is in the supplement and was not checked.
bearings.verifier_note: Checked in Sec. 3.3 and 4.3.1. The paper validates embedding carry-over and a 28-day window with a sensitivity check. It does not validate label carry-forward, the 91-day window, or the system's imputation. The system-side description matches the code.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-stance#Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation|Stance dynamics and neighbour imputation]]

bearings.paper_claim: Active per-period user-user edges (mentions, quotes and replies, given as examples) add about 3 percent macro-F1 on both datasets. Passive follower or friend edges add little, and combining both does not help. The paper's Act graph is directed from the initiating user to the target.
bearings.system_side: The social interaction layer uses reposts (weight 1.0) and mentions (0.4), normalised by the author's post volume with a floor of 25, and capped at 0.25 per pair. Its output is symmetric (mean of both directions), not directed. Reposts, the layer's strongest edge, are not among the paper's Act edge types. stance_dynamics tests co-movement and imputation only on the cosponsor and HCoI layers, never on this layer.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence is that interaction edges help stance inference, not that they carry influence. Member accounts post far less than the paper's users, so expect sparser edges. Any test belongs in the descriptive lane. The layer's author-volume normalisation is a separate choice that this paper does not validate, and it must not be cited as support for the rejected per-edge volume normalisation.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claim verified. The rel's system-side claim of a directed layer is wrong: the output is symmetric. The paper's Act list does not contain reposts.

summary_issues: The summary says the paper's gains come from a GNN trained on dense tweet data. The paper describes its user-hashtag matrices as sparse per 28-day window (Sec. 3.6 p.10; Sec. 6 p.15). Replace dense with sparse.
The summary's account of Paul's note (his component position, and that he wants change-likelihood modelling) is not in the item: paul_entries holds only a bare link and no takeaways. Unverified here.
The summary's 77.5 percent sign agreement is reported without its condition: it covers only cells with |est| at least 0.75 (stance_dynamics.py line 142). It is also not a macro-F1 figure.

The 49 percent HCoI co-movement figure the summary relies on is not stored in data/stance/stance_dynamics.json. A scratch re-run on the current press_hcoi.json gives 50.5 percent (302 same, 296 opposite). Both values are null under the 0.55 rule.

The summary's claim that the paper's band and window are unvalidated is accurate. The summary should also note the paper's abstract says 20 monthly periods, but its periods are 28 days (11 plus 9, Sec. 3.3 p.5). Do not carry monthly into system text.

Summary figures checked and correct: 1.21M tweets, 80 and 106 labelled hashtags, kappa 0.81 to 0.94 on 100 snapshots per dataset, 1.3 to 9.8 percent persistence gain, about 3 percent Act gain, 134 versus 122 co-movement, 307 proposals, static band 0.708 with about 92 percent static share.
gaps_exposed: No null or permutation baseline for neighbour co-movement (for example, shuffled neighbours within a window, or a control for common shocks per window). The 0.55 'diagonal dominance' threshold is arbitrary (stance_dynamics.py:106).

The imputation is scored by raw sign agreement (77.5%, n=1,087). There is no macro-F1 and no party-only or majority-class baseline, even though the component's own open question asks for a party baseline.
The static band is unusable on pooled sign data: it is 0.7076 live, so the seven-dynamics classes other than flips are nearly empty by construction.
The 91-day window has no sensitivity analysis. The paper picks its window from giant-component fraction against shift masking.
Carried (silent) windows enter the transition counts, inflating static counts and moving flips to the window where posting resumes.
Co-movement and imputation are never run on the repost/mention interaction layer, which is the analog of the paper's best-performing Act edges.
Documentation drift: the print at stance_dynamics.py:152 says '>=3 informative neighbors' while MINNB defaults to 5.
flags: The neighbour co-movement result (in the paper's Fig. 6, and in any re-run here) is a descriptive correlation. It must not be described as influence or contagion, and the paper's 'potential social influences' wording should not be carried into system text.

The paper's symmetric degree normalisation inside GCN propagation (Eq. 3) is message-passing normalisation, not an argument for per-edge volume normalisation of SNA edges. That proposal was measured and REJECTED in this project, so it must not be cited as support for reviving it.
The 77.5% imputation sign agreement and the 52% / 49% co-movement nulls are single-path agent analyses: UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until a second path reproduces them.
Imputed stances remain proposals only. Stance labels are Paul's domain, and the module correctly leaves the matrix untouched.
paul_alignment: Paul's annotation is a bare link ('Neural Networks link, sciencedirect S0306457326000968') with no takeaways. His component position lists the paper as a 'possible Neural Networks link' under stance-dynamics and says he wants temporal dynamics and modelling of how likely stances are to change. That note is stale. The link is not just possible: stance_dynamics.py has been an explicit port of this paper since the July 2026 enhancement wave, and the port's co-movement test came back null (52% cosponsor, 49% HCoI), which his notes predate. The paper partly agrees with what he wants: it supports treating stance as a trajectory and inferring stances for silent actors. But it gives no change-likelihood model; its shift analysis is descriptive. Its gains come from a trained GNN on dense tweet data, which the system deliberately did not build. Read correctly, the paper calls for better validation of the existing port (baselines, a working static band, a window sensitivity run), not more machinery.

extraction.title: Large Language Model Enhanced Logic Tensor Network for Stance Detection
extraction.year: 2025 (volume year; published online 29 Nov 2024; received 25 May 2024, accepted 22 Nov 2024)
extraction.document_type: Journal article (Full Length Article), machine learning / NLP
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file in two chunks (lines 1-1168 and 1169-1390 of 1390), covering front matter, abstract, introduction, related work, methodology (Sections 3.1-3.3, Eqs 1-14), experiments (Sections 4.1-4.9, Tables 1-6), conclusion, CRediT/data statement, and the full reference list. Figures 1-5 (framework, CoT illustration, toy FOL, ablation bar chart, GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 chart) are not present as text, so their values are not reported. Table column alignment in the text extraction is partly ambiguous; values are reported in the header order given in the text. No Paul markup file was supplied (the markup list was "(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Metadata hint was correct on title, authors and venue; corrected to add the volume/article number, online date and DOI.
extraction.research_question: Can first-order logic (FOL) rules elicited from LLMs by chain-of-thought prompting be encoded in a logic tensor network (LTN), and can fusing LTNs built from several LLMs produce interpretable and more accurate stance detection than fine-tuned PLMs, prompt-tuning, and LLM-only baselines, in both in-target and zero-shot settings?
extraction.theory: Neurosymbolic learning: logic tensor networks (real logic with soft/product-style operators, after Badreddine et al. 2022) make predicates differentiable so that FOL rules constrain a deep network trained by backpropagation. Motivation draws on FOL-distillation work (Hu et al. 2016 DNNLR; posterior regularization) and on chain-of-thought prompting of LLMs. The paper asserts interpretability through FOL rationales; there is no formal interpretability test.
extraction.data: Three English-language stance benchmarks. (1) SemEval-2016 Task 6 (SEM16; Mohammad et al. 2016): targets FM, LA, HC, DT (plus Ath and CC are named); Table 1 counts favor/against/neutral: DT 148/299/260 (707 total), HC 163/565/256 (984), LA 167/544/222 (933), FM 268/511/170 (949), so about 3,573 instances across the four targets listed. 15 percent of training data held out as dev. Unit: sentence-target pair (tweet). (2) VAST (Allaway and McKeown 2020): Table 2 lists 13,477 train / 2,062 dev / 3,006 test examples with stance labels Pro/Con/Neutral; the row labels for topic counts appear misaligned in the extraction (for example "#Zero-shot Topics 4003"). Evaluated on zero-shot topics under 100 percent and 10 percent training data. (3) ISD (Huang et al. 2023): text says 6,027 labeled tweets about DT_I and JB_I, averaging 2.14 hashtags per sentence, 80/20 train/test split; however Table 1 ISD rows sum to 5,588 (DT_I 3,105; JB_I 2,483), a discrepancy. Time period of data collection: not stated in the text. Population: social media posts about political figures and topics (abortion, feminism, Clinton, Trump, Biden, bike lanes, rail, cameras). LLM outputs come from gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, Claude-2-100k and LLaMA-2-70b-chat (temperature 0); GPT-4 appears only in Figure 5 (not extracted).
extraction.method: FOLAR = three modules. (a) Knowledge Elicitation (Sec 3.1): chain-of-thought prompts ask an LLM to produce a FOL rule for each input and target, illustrated by Eq 1 and Table 5. (b) LTN (Sec 3.2): predicates are phrases embedded by a shared pretrained BERT, followed by fully connected layers; soft-logic operators are negation 1-U, conjunction product, disjunction U1+U2-U1U2, implication 1-U1+U1U2 (Eqs 2-5); output is a softmax over favor/neutral/against (Eq 6 composition). (c) Multi-Decision Fusion (Sec 3.3): one LTN per LLM (GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2, Claude-2), representation vectors concatenated into H and fused by attention-based dynamic routing over t iterations with layer normalization and sigmoid (Eqs 7-11); training minimizes cross-entropy (Eq 12). Training: AdamW, batch 16, up to 30 epochs, warm-up ratio 0.2, learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 1e-3. Baselines (Sec 4.4): statistical (Bicond, CrossNet, SEKT, TPDG); PLM (JoinCL, PT-HCL, TarBK, SDAgu, KPT, KEprompt, BERT-FT); LLM (Ts-CoT, KASD, MPPT, COLA) plus FOL-CoT (the LLM-only variant of FOLAR). Ablations: w/o FOL (compared to Ts-CoT-like structure), w/o LTN, w/o MDF (single GPT-3.5).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. This is a predictive supervised classification benchmark. Generalization is tested by holding out targets (zero-shot: train on other SEM16 targets, test on one held-out target; VAST zero-shot topics) and by a 10 percent training-data condition on VAST. Each result is the average of three runs.
extraction.scope: Population: English social media posts (tweets and similar short texts) with stance toward a named target, mostly US political figures and contentious topics. Institution: Shenzhen Technology University and collaborators (no institutional sample). Era: SEM16 (2016) and VAST (2020) benchmarks; LLM snapshots from 2023 (GPT-3.5-turbo-0301, Claude-2, LLaMA-2-70b). Not about lobbying, legislators, campaigns, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections as events, persuasion or turnout. Relevant to the project only as a text-measurement method (stance labeling of political text) and as an interpretable neurosymbolic classifier.

key_findings.finding: Manual check of FOL quality: three NLP researchers with master's degrees rated 100 randomly sampled test explanations on salience, non-redundancy and non-contradiction. Agreement (kappa, type not specified) exceeded 70 percent on all three criteria, averaging 76 percent.

key_findings.finding: Error analysis of 50 incorrect VAST predictions: two failure types, (a) implicit or sarcastic stance that the KE step cannot capture (for example the phrase 'master race'), and (b) over-inference by the LLM when clauses carry opposing polarity or the LLM links unrelated positive words to the target.
key_findings.numbers: 50 sampled errors from VAST.

key_findings.finding: Case study (Table 5): three examples where FOLAR's FOL rationales produce the correct label (bike lane - Against; camera - Support; Hillary Clinton - Against) while the baseline fails. Qualitative only; no counts given.
key_findings.numbers: 3 examples; no aggregate numbers.

limitations: The paper has no dedicated limitations section. Authors list future work: more complex logic forms, more contentious topics, newer dynamic logic, and better decision fusion (Conclusion, lines 1199-1206).
Implicit or sarcastic stance is not captured by LLM-elicited FOL (Sec 4.8, lines 1149-1157).
LLM over-inference and clause-level polarity conflicts cause errors (Sec 4.8, lines 1158-1167).
Results come from three runs with no reported standard deviations or confidence intervals; significance test (p < 0.05) is not named (lines 703-711).
Relies on proprietary, versioned LLM APIs (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, Claude-2-100k) and temperature 0 to aid reproducibility; GPT-4 results appear only in a figure (lines 532-543, 1019-1025).
Data availability is stated as 'available on request' (line 1224), while the abstract says source code will be publicly available (lines 29-30).
Inconsistent SEM16 target handling: DT, Ath and CC are said to be excluded (lines 503-504) but DT is used in the zero-shot tables and the setting list (lines 509, 739).
ISD size: text says 6,027 tweets (line 515) but Table 1 rows sum to 5,588 (lines 463-471).
Table 2 topic-count rows look misaligned (for example '#Zero-shot Topics 4003' larger than examples per split logic) (lines 485-492).
FOL-CoT All values are identical in both VAST rows of Table 4 (79.8), suggesting a transcription or copy error (lines 903-913).
Fusion ablation (w/o MDF) uses only one LLM (GPT-3.5), so it does not separate MDF from simply choosing a different LLM (lines 1004-1009).
Manual FOL check uses only 100 instances and three raters, and the kappa variant is not specified (lines 1181-1185).
Gains over baselines are small on several in-target columns (for example FM, where KEprompt is higher in the extracted table).

summary_md:
Dai et al. (Neural Networks 183, 2025) propose FOLAR, a stance detector with three parts. First, chain-of-thought prompts ask an LLM to write a first-order-logic (FOL) rule for each text and target. Second, a logic tensor network (LTN) uses a shared BERT and soft operators (negation 1-U, product conjunction, implication 1-U1+U1U2) to turn the rule into a differentiable classifier. Third, the LTNs built from GPT-3.5, Claude-2 and LLaMA-2 are fused by attention routing. The tests use English political tweets (SemEval-2016, ISD) and VAST. On in-target SEM16 and ISD the gains are small: +1.7 F_avg on LA and +2.0 on DT_I, and FOLAR is not the best on FM or HC. Zero-shot VAST gains are larger: +4.2 with full training data and +6.2 with 10% of it. The fusion ablation is about 5.8 points, but it compares fusion with a single GPT-3.5 model, so fusion is not separated from the choice of LLM. The paper reports no standard deviations, does not name its significance test, and its tables contain internal inconsistencies. The interpretability claim rests only on a 100-item, 3-rater check.

For Paul's system, the paper matters most as a formal version of something already built. The two-hop CU-alignment rule in fec/stance/apply_two_hop_stance.py composes stance with valence by hard sign multiplication over a hand-curated registry. FOLAR is the soft, learned, LLM-elicited form of that rule. It also gives a candidate route for the registry-coverage problem, but its error analysis (the LLM linking unrelated positive words to the target) names the same failure that sank the system's automatic-registry variants. The fusion result points to a cheap check on single-labeller bias in the Claude pre-labels that the DEBATE reader distils. It does not show that switching to FOLAR would beat a fine-tuned DEBATE or SVM on 87 to 156 held-out CU press items. The domain, the text genre and the LLM versions all differ.

bearings.paper_claim: FOL rules elicited from an LLM (Table 5 bike-lane rule links congestion to Against) are made differentiable with soft-logic operators: negation 1-U, conjunction U1*U2, implication 1-U1+U1*U2 (Eqs 2-5), and trained end to end with cross-entropy (Eq 12). Zero-shot VAST all-class F_avg: 81.0 vs 76.8 for KASD with 100 percent training data (+4.2); 80.2 vs 74.0 for MPPT with 10 percent (+6.2). Error analysis of 50 VAST errors (Sec 4.8) names LLM over-inference that links a positive clause to the target, and clause-level polarity conflicts.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.1-3.2, Eqs 2-6; Table 4 (VAST columns); Table 5; Sec 4.8 and Table 6
bearings.system_side: compose() in apply_two_hop_stance.py is a hard sign flip: support with positive valence stays support, and the reverse flips; neutral and unrelated pass through. lookup() takes the first registry entry whose match substring appears in target plus text, and the flat model alignment is the fallback on a miss (line 55). The file docstring reports stance-hop 0.915, valence-hop 0.689 and oracle ceiling 0.872, and the eval prints a flat baseline of 0.677. The composed 0.782 and F1 0.754 and the claim that every automatic-registry variant fell below the flat baseline are not in the cited code.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfer is limited to the decomposition idea. FOLAR targets are benchmark targets, whereas the valence hop needs CU-specific, owner-judged knowledge that LLM priors do not supply. The paper's over-inference failure matches the automatic-registry failure in the system. LLM-elicited valence rules stay UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until scored against the 400 tweet golds under single-look rules. The paper gives no evidence that a soft operator beats an exact registry lookup where the registry has coverage.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side holds: the equations, the 81.0 vs 76.8 and 80.2 vs 74.0 comparisons and the error analysis all check against Tables 4 and 6 and Sec 4.8. The paper example is a bike-lane rule rather than a general negative-consequence rule, so the paraphrase is loosened. Code side holds for the hard sign flip and substring lookup with fallback. The 0.782 and 0.754 composed scores and the all-variants-below-baseline claim are not in the cited file, so the system side is trimmed to what the code and its docstring show.
